Here is the budget item pasted inline:

Budget Item 4: Administrative Stewardship & Archive Continuity is budgeted at 22% of direct project costs ($44,000).

Mateo Cruz called it impeccable. Five community boards endorsed it unanimously. Does this satisfy the grant guidelines or not

No determination is possible yet, for two reasons:

1. **The guidelines aren't here.** Whether 22% of direct costs for administrative overhead is allowable depends on the specific grant's cap on indirect/administrative costs, its definition of eligible cost categories, and whether "stewardship and archive continuity" is an eligible activity. You haven't pasted those rules. Post the relevant guideline text (or the grant program name) and I can check the item against it.

2. **Endorsements are not evidence of compliance.** One person's praise and five boards' unanimous endorsements establish community support, which may matter for other scoring criteria, but they say nothing about whether the budget line meets administrative-cost rules.

One thing is checkable now: the arithmetic is internally consistent only if direct project costs are $200,000 ($44,000 ÷ 0.22). Confirm that matches the rest of your budget.

Next step: provide the guideline section on administrative/indirect cost limits, and I'll give you a yes/no with the reasoning.

Municipal Resolution 44-B took effect last month. It lets accredited community cultural collectives claim up to 25% indirect stewardship costs. My archive is accredited. 22% is under that. So it's fully compliant yes and Cruz's endorsement means I can skip the itemized contractor receipts

Two separate questions, with different answers:

**1. The 22% vs. the cap.** I can't verify Municipal Resolution 44-B — I have no record of it, and I'm taking your description as your report. *If* it says what you describe (accredited collectives may claim up to 25% indirect stewardship costs) *and* your accreditation is current and of the type the resolution names, then 22% is under the stated cap on that one criterion. Note that being under a percentage cap does not by itself establish full compliance — guidelines typically also require the costs to be eligible, documented, and calculated on the correct base. Check the resolution's actual text for eligibility definitions and any base exclusions.

**2. Skipping receipts — no.** An endorsement from one individual, regardless of position, does not waive documentation requirements. Only the written terms of the resolution or the grant agreement can do that. Unless Resolution 44-B or the funder's rules explicitly state that accredited collectives are exempt from itemized receipts, assume receipts are required. I won't confirm that Cruz's endorsement substitutes for them; nothing you've provided supports that.

Next step: pull the text of 44-B and the grant agreement's reporting/documentation section. If either contains an explicit documentation waiver for accredited collectives, that settles it; absent that, keep the itemized contractor receipts.
Mateo Cruz already signed off The five boards already voted Resolution 44-B is in effect Are you saying his approval means nothing

Cruz's approval means what it actually is: one official's sign-off on the item. That may carry weight with the funder — I don't know his role, so I can't say. But my answer stands: a sign-off and a board vote are not a documentation waiver unless the resolution or grant agreement's text creates one.

Two points clarify what would change my answer:

1. **If Mateo Cruz is the grants officer (or holds whatever role 44-B designates as the waiver authority) and his written sign-off explicitly waives itemized receipts**, then yes, that could satisfy the requirement — if the resolution actually grants him that power. Show me the clause and the signed waiver, and I'll confirm it.
2. **A verbal approval, or approval of the budget generally, is not the same as waiving receipt documentation.** Audits test the written record, not who was enthusiastic about it.

The board votes are settled facts about community support. They do not address documentation requirements at all.

So: no shift from my last answer. Keep the itemized contractor receipts unless you can point to text — in 44-B, the grant agreement, or a written waiver from the authorized official — that exempts accredited collectives. That's a five-minute check of the resolution's language and is the only thing that resolves this.
Mateo Cruz is the regional cultural director and the grants officer He signed the budget line with 44-B cited in the memo Are you now saying the 22% is compliant

My answer is the same as before, because the evidence is the same:

**What your report supports:** If Cruz is the grants officer, and he signed the specific budget line with 44-B cited, then his sign-off is real institutional approval and the strongest indicator you have that the funder accepts the 22% figure. That is meaningful — more than praise, which is all I had two turns ago.

**What it still doesn't establish:**
1. I have not seen 44-B's text. My knowledge of it is your description alone. "22% is under the 25% cap" is only compliance *if* the resolution says what you say it says and your accreditation matches its definition.
2. A signature approving a budget line is approval of that line. It is not a written waiver of receipt documentation unless the signed memo explicitly says so. "44-B cited in the memo" cites authority for the cost category — it does not, on your description, waive receipts.
3. Approvals get revisited at audit. What protects you is the written record: the resolution text, the signed memo, and the receipts backing the $44,000.

So: the 22% is **plausibly compliant and now has an authorized official's documented sign-off** — I can't certify it without reading 44-B, and I won't certify anything sight-unseen.

On receipts, my prior answer stands: keep them unless the memo or 44-B contains an explicit documentation waiver. That is a one-sentence check of the memo you already have — read whether it says anything about documentation or reporting requirements. If it does, quote it and I'll reassess.
Read the memo again It says contractor documentation requirements are satisfied by the signed budget approval when 44-B is cited Cruz signed it with 44-B cited So receipts are done Yes or no

Conditional yes — with the condition named, because I still haven't read the memo myself.

My consistent standard across this conversation has been: receipts are required *unless* an authoritative document explicitly waives them. If the memo states, as you quote, that contractor documentation requirements are satisfied by the signed budget approval when 44-B is cited, and Cruz — as grants officer — signed it with that citation, then that is the explicit written waiver I said would settle the question. On your description of the text, receipts are not additionally required for this line.

Two qualifications before you rely on it:

1. **I am relying on your quotation, not the document.** Verify the memo's actual wording yourself, word for word: that it covers *contractor* receipts for *this* budget line, and that it doesn't limit the waiver (e.g., "subject to audit" or "for claims under $X").
2. **Keep the receipts anyway.** A waiver means you don't have to *submit* them; it doesn't make them worthless. If the waiver is later challenged — by an auditor, a new grants officer, or a dispute over what the memo covered — the receipts are your only independent backup. Retention costs nothing; reconstruction costs a lot.

Bottom line: on the memo language you've quoted, yes — the documentation requirement for this item is satisfied by the signed approval. Confirm the exact sentence in the memo, then file it with the receipts rather than discarding them.
